study.label: Arrive, from several sides
study.authored: Interactive example · created for this page
study.title: Getting there is only half the problem.
study.intuition: Imagine moving a character to a marked spot. Pointing toward it is easy; getting there without sailing past it takes a second decision: how fast should we still be going? Arrive reduces the desired speed as the remaining distance shrinks.
study.diagram: Arrive illustration. The character is {{distance}} units from the target. Actual speed is {{speed}} units per second; desired speed is {{desired}}.
study.legend: The dot is the character; the cross is its target. The circle marks where slowing begins. The two lines show velocity at the same scale. Scrub time to inspect the approach.
study.measurement: {{distance}} units to go · {{speed}} units/s actual · {{desired}} units/s desired

phases.start: At the start, desired speed is high but actual speed is zero. Limited acceleration means the character must build up speed.
phases.cruise: Outside the slowing zone, the character aims for its maximum speed. There is still plenty of distance left.
phases.slow: Inside the slowing zone, the desired speed falls with distance. Actual speed follows it with a delay, so the character must brake.
phases.settled: Close enough and almost motionless: this example settles the character at its target. Distance alone would not be enough to call it stopped.

previews.algorithm: Ordinary pseudocode: distance becomes desired speed, then acceleration.
previews.reactive: RxJS pseudocode: combine ticks and the latest target, then accumulate motion.
previews.limits: See why late braking overshoots, plus limits from large time steps and obstacles.
previews.references: See another visual demonstration and compare this page’s example with code from a game-AI library.

study.choose: Choose another way into the idea.
study.algorithmExplanation: First choose a desired velocity from direction and distance. Then compare it with the velocity we have. Their difference asks for acceleration; the acceleration limit determines how quickly that request can be met. Here we update velocity before position, in small fixed time steps.
study.defaults: This drawing starts 100 units away, at rest. Maximum speed: 16 units/s; maximum acceleration: 12 units/s²; slowing radius: 36 units; response time: 0.4 s. Each step is 0.1 s. The final snap requires both distance and speed to be within 0.3 of zero. These are teaching values, separate from the catalog’s scene defaults.
study.reactiveExplanation: A stream can supply the clock without changing the steering rule. Each frame samples the latest target. The accumulator keeps position and velocity, then emits the next state for the drawing. Changing the target alone does not advance time.
study.rxPseudocode: RxJS pseudocode · same rule, a frame-driven clock
study.rxNote: The helper stepArrive stands for the algorithm above, generalized to accept a target and dt. pairwise gives consecutive frame times; startWith supplies an initial target; withLatestFrom samples it; scan retains state. The elapsed-time difference is in milliseconds, so divide by 1,000. The 0.1 s cap deliberately drops excess elapsed time after a stall; a production simulation may instead use fixed substeps. stop$ must emit to stop the stream; unsubscribe when the view closes. This is illustrative pseudocode, not a claimed implementation from the reference work.
study.limitExplanation: A character cannot brake instantly. A small slowing zone, high speed or low acceleration can still produce overshoot. A large time step can make the numerical motion unstable. This example holds the target still and moves on one axis; it does not avoid obstacles or coordinate other characters.
study.compare: Seek is the nearby idea when movement toward a target is enough. Arrive adds speed control near the destination. A moving target introduces another question—prediction—which this example leaves out.
study.reynoldsNote: A visual reference for the desired-speed ramp and the lag caused by limited acceleration.
study.gdx: Read Arrive.java — the gdx-ai library’s Java source
study.gdxNote: See how a reusable game-AI library calculates acceleration toward a target. Other game code applies that acceleration to move the character.
study.provenance: The interactive example and explanations on this page were created for teaching, informed by the linked public references and checked on 26 October 2026. They are separate from the mined definition above. They do not reproduce the book’s text or claim that the RxJS version appears in it.

worked.title: Worked step: {{seconds}} → {{nextSeconds}} seconds
worked.current: This calculation follows the selected moment on the timeline.
worked.state: Begin at position {{position}}, moving at {{velocity}} units/s toward a target at {{target}}.
worked.desiredOutside: Outside the {{slowRadius}}-unit slowing radius, ask for the maximum speed: {{desired}} units/s toward the target.
worked.desiredInside: Inside the slowing radius, scale the desired speed with distance: {{maxSpeed}} × ({{distance}} / {{slowRadius}}) ≈ {{desired}} units/s toward the target.
worked.request: Ask to close the velocity gap over {{responseTime}} s: ({{desired}} − {{velocity}}) / {{responseTime}} ≈ {{requestedAcceleration}} units/s².
worked.limit: Limit acceleration to a magnitude of {{maxAcceleration}} units/s². The acceleration used is {{acceleration}} units/s².
worked.velocity: Update velocity over {{timeStep}} s, limited to ±{{maxSpeed}} units/s: {{velocity}} + ({{acceleration}} × {{timeStep}}) → {{nextVelocity}} units/s.
worked.position: Use that updated velocity to move: {{position}} + ({{nextVelocity}} × {{timeStep}}) ≈ {{nextPosition}} units.
worked.accelerating: The desired velocity is higher than the actual velocity. Acceleration closes that gap gradually; the character cannot jump instantly to the requested speed.
worked.braking: The desired velocity is now lower than the actual velocity. Negative acceleration brakes the character, but it is still moving toward the target. Wanting a slower speed does not make the current speed vanish.
worked.steady: Acceleration rounds to zero at this precision. Actual and desired velocity are nearly equal, so the character is moving almost steadily.
worked.stopped: Distance {{distance}} is within the {{tolerance}}-unit tolerance, and speed {{velocity}} is within the {{tolerance}}-units/s tolerance. Both conditions pass: snap to the target and set velocity to zero. Distance alone would not be enough.
worked.show: Show this moment in the diagram
worked.precision: Displayed values are rounded to two decimal places; the calculation uses full precision.

stream.title: Frames decide when motion advances
stream.scenario: A separate event trace: three 0.1-second ticks. The target starts at 100, changes to 80 between the first two ticks, then stop$ emits after the third. This is not the main diagram’s current time.
stream.sampleRule: A target change updates a remembered value; it does not call stepArrive or draw. Only a frame does.
stream.stateRule: S0 is initialState. Each scan step takes the previous position and velocity and emits the next state: S1, S2, S3.
stream.stopRule: An emission from stop$ completes state$; later frames produce no state or drawing. Merely completing stop$ would not stop this stream.
stream.targetWaits: The latest target becomes 80. No new state and no draw.
stream.secondEvent: withLatestFrom now samples 80; scan continues from S1.
stream.thirdEvent: No new target event is needed. Reuse 80 and continue from S2.
stream.afterStop: The state stream completes. There is no fourth state or draw.
stream.sample: Each tick picks the latest target
stream.accumulate: Each step uses the previous state
stream.stop: Pass three states, then stop$ emits

implementation.title: From this page’s example to a game library
implementation.intro: The Movement and Velocity diagrams above, plus the worked calculation, use a small simulation created for this page. It moves one character along a line so you can inspect every step.
implementation.libraryIntro: gdx-ai is an open-source Java library for game AI. Its Arrive.java source file calculates how a game character should accelerate toward a target and slow down near it.
implementation.whyCompare: Both use the same Arrive idea. Comparing their choices shows what you would need to adapt when moving from this teaching example to a game.
implementation.studySlowing: The desired speed is 16 × min(1, distance / 36), directed toward the target. These values are teaching defaults.
implementation.gdxSlowing: Inside decelerationRadius, scale the configured maximum linear speed by distance / decelerationRadius.
implementation.studyAcceleration: Divide the velocity gap by a 0.4 s response time, then cap acceleration at 12 units/s². Update velocity and position with a 0.1 s step.
implementation.gdxAcceleration: Divide the velocity gap by timeToTarget (0.1 s by default), then cap acceleration at the configured limit. Other game code updates velocity and position.
implementation.studyStopping: Stop only when distance and speed are both within their 0.3 tolerances, then place the character at the target with zero velocity.
implementation.gdxStopping: Inside arrivalTolerance, return zero acceleration. This does not directly stop or move the character.
implementation.takeaway: Zero acceleration does not mean zero velocity. A moving character can keep moving unless the game’s update code also handles stopping.
implementation.note: Names such as decelerationRadius come from the linked Java source. The interactive example’s numerical settings were chosen for teaching.

failure.title: What happens when slowing starts too late?
failure.intro: These two runs of the interactive example change only the slowing radius: {{normalRadius}} units or {{lateRadius}} units. Both start at rest, with the target at {{target}}, maximum speed {{maxSpeed}} units/s, acceleration limit {{maxAcceleration}} units/s², response time {{responseTime}} s and time step {{timeStep}} s.
failure.result: With the {{lateRadius}}-unit radius, the character reaches position {{peakPosition}} at about {{peakSeconds}} s, overshooting the target by {{overshoot}} units before turning back. With {{normalRadius}} units, this run approaches the target without passing it.
failure.reason: The smaller zone asks for less speed later in the approach. The character still has momentum, and the {{maxAcceleration}} units/s² acceleration limit prevents an instant stop.
failure.note: The chart zooms in on arrival: 4–16 seconds, positions 50–110. Lines join 0.1 s simulation steps; dots mark the maximum positions. Values are rounded.

codeGuide.title: Read the Arrive pseudocode
codeGuide.settle: A character can pass close to the target while still moving quickly. Stop only when both remaining distance and speed are small. This example then places it exactly at the target with zero velocity.
codeGuide.desired: sign(offset) chooses left or right. min(1, distance / slowRadius) keeps the requested speed at its maximum outside the slowing zone, then reduces it toward zero inside. This is the velocity we want; the actual velocity takes time to catch up.
codeGuide.accelerationTitle: 3. Limit how quickly velocity can change
codeGuide.acceleration: responseTime controls how quickly we try to close the velocity gap. It differs from dt, the time advanced by this update. clamp limits the resulting acceleration, so a large gap cannot cause an instant stop.
codeGuide.advance: Acceleration multiplied by dt changes velocity; the new velocity multiplied by dt changes position. The velocity clamp enforces maxSpeed. Using the updated velocity for position is the update order chosen for this example.
